prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators remain my first choice, and the opening ballots support it: seven of eight members ranked B028, three of them first and five in their top three, which is the broadest support on the shortlist, although support is not itself evidence of merit. The merit is that bulk band topology forces protected edge and surface states, a genuinely new class of quantum matter. The chain is clear: Kane and Mele's 2005 Z2 theory and quantum spin Hall prediction, then Molenkamp's HgTe observation of edge transport, then the three-dimensional materials. The discovery is original, independently confirmed over about two decades, and has spread into photonics, superconductivity and computational materials search. That is the kind of discovery-centred case I favour: a clear phenomenon first, and then the people behind it.
statement.case_against: The credited list leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (the HgTe proposal) and Fu, Moore and Balents, so any prize from these names is a partial picture. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions may be read as having already covered part of this territory, and some will feel the field is more a conceptual framework than one discrete discovery. Whichever three of Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan we choose, one strong claimant is excluded, and I cannot verify exact priority from the supplied record.

responses.point: Credit Kane and Mele for the theory and Molenkamp for the first experimental observation, leaving Hasan's 3D ARPES work out because of the three-person limit.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge to my opening trio. I proposed Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to cover theory, 2D experiment and 3D experiment, but that treats Kane and Mele as separable when they are not: the Z2 invariant and the graphene quantum spin Hall proposal are a joint work, and a citation that names Kane without Mele would be hard to defend. I now move to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. I still regard Hasan's 3D identification as decisive for the field, and I would want the citation to be worded so that the 2D result is not presented as the whole discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because a continuum band-structure prediction preceded and guided a field-defining experiment, and also ranks B028 second with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan.
responses.response: I agree that B046 is a strong prediction-then-experiment case and I rank it as a serious alternative. My reservations are maturity and allocation. The pairing mechanism is unsettled and the experiments are only about eight years old, and by your own account the third slot among Andrei, Bistritzer and others is unresolved. B028 has the clearer attribution chain and a longer record of independent confirmation. I also differ on Hasan: your subset prefers him to Mele, but I now think that omitting a co-originator of the Z2 theory is the weaker choice.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: a clean two-person case, Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's record accuracy, with a natural link to the earlier frequency-comb prize and a redefinition of the second under discussion.
responses.response: I agree that B034 is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and I ranked it fourth only because it is a refinement of metrology that the 2005 and 2012 prizes opened. I do not share the view that a possible redefinition of the second adds to the merit; the prize should rest on what was discovered or achieved, not on an administrative event. I note your disclosure of links to the Hall-lab environment. B034 is the best fallback if the committee judges the topological-insulator allocation too contested.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy first, weighing the instrumental achievement and the source associations, while acknowledging that a single-name prize for a collaboration is a problem.
responses.response: I ranked B005 second and value it for the same reason: a clear observable and a new window on cosmic-ray accelerators. But your own attribution caveat is, I think, decisive for this round. A one-laureate prize for a large collaboration, with AMANDA and the detector and analysis teams uncredited in the supplied names, is fragile, and only two of us ranked it at all. It remains a discovery I would want to see recognised, but not in the form this ballot can currently support.

uncertainties: Whether Mele or Hasan should hold the third slot, and how the committee words a citation that stays faithful to both the 2D and 3D parts of the discovery.
How much the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against recognising this specific discovery.
Exact priority among the 2005-2008 theory and experiment papers, which I rely on recalled history for.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) is tied to any shortlisted candidate.
